name: MLX-native backend + speculative (draft-model) decoding for Apple Silicon
what_it_is: Two related, currently-shipping capabilities. (1) Apple's MLX / mlx-lm exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server whose primary endpoint is `/v1/chat/completions` (plus `/v1/models`), and that server natively supports speculative decoding via a `draft_model` parameter (a smaller model, settable to null to unload) and a `num_draft_tokens` parameter (how many tokens the draft predicts at once, default 3). The mlx-lm README also documents generation, chat, quantization, LoRA/full fine-tuning, and distributed inference; the server docs warn it 'is not recommended for production as it only implements basic security checks.' (2) llama.cpp has broad speculative-decoding support in llama-cli/llama-server, selected with `--spec-type` and a draft model via `--spec-draft-model`/`-md`, tuned with `--spec-draft-n-max` (default 3) and `--spec-draft-n-min`, and offering many draft strategies: `draft-simple` (small draft model), `draft-eagle3` (reads target hidden states), `draft-dflash` (whole draft block in one forward pass), `draft-dspark`, and n-gram variants (`ngram-cache`, `ngram-simple`, `ngram-map-k`, `ngram-map-k4v`, `ngram-mod`). EAGLE-3/DFlash drafts inherit the target's tokenizer via `--target-model-dir`. Speedup is gated by the draft acceptance rate (the docs show example rates of 0.576 and 0.703).
real_precedent: mlx-lm OpenAI-compatible server with `draft_model` + `num_draft_tokens` speculative-decoding params: https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/main/mlx_lm/SERVER.md . mlx-lm project scope (generate/chat/quantize/fine-tune/distributed): https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm . llama.cpp speculative-decoding flags and draft types: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/speculative.md . Community-reported real-world llama.cpp speculative speedups and failure cases: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/10466
evidence_of_impact: llama.cpp's own docs report acceptance rates of 0.576 (171/297) and 0.703 (90/128), confirming that gains are acceptance-rate-bound: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/speculative.md . Community benchmarks in the llama.cpp discussion report the effect is real but uneven and task-dependent: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B + 0.5B draft ~2.9x and Qwen2.5-Coder-14B + 0.5B draft ~2.5x on coding, Llama-3.1-8B + 1B draft ~1.83x, but only ~1.4x on general Qwen2.5-14B text, and explicitly 'never any speculative decoding speedup' for Gemma-2-9B drafted by Gemma-2-2B; returns degrade past a 0.5B draft and become 'not really useful at 3B' (tested on RTX 4070-class GPUs): https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/10466 . mlx-lm ships draft-model support in its server as a documented, first-class option: https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/main/mlx_lm/SERVER.md . [uncertain] Apple-Silicon-specific speculative speedup magnitudes (e.g. MTP/ReDrafter 2.x claims) surfaced only in unfetched secondary blogs/preprints and are NOT verified here; the fetched hardware evidence is GPU (RTX-class), not Apple Silicon.
applicability_to_agentdyno: AgentDyno already normalizes multiple engines (llama-server + Ollama) behind a stable OpenAI-style gateway at 127.0.0.1:8403/v1. Because mlx-lm's server is itself OpenAI-compatible on `/v1/chat/completions`, adding it as a third backend (`dyno serve --backend mlx`, launched/proxied like the existing llama-server process) is architecturally low-friction and is the single most Apple-Silicon-native option AgentDyno could offer. Two concrete wins: (a) `dyno scan`/`dyno fit` already profile the user's Mac -- extend them to recommend a *draft-model pairing* (matching-tokenizer small model) and to auto-emit the correct spec-decode config (`--spec-draft-model` for llama-server, `draft_model`/`num_draft_tokens` for mlx-lm); (b) turn AgentDyno's core identity -- an empirical *verification bench* -- onto speculative decoding itself: since the fetched evidence shows speedups swing from ~2.9x to actively negative depending on the exact model/draft/task pair and hardware, a `dyno` command that actually measures tokens/sec with vs. without the draft on the user's own machine (and refuses to enable it when it regresses) is a genuinely differentiated, hard-to-fake capability that neither a static fit-calculator nor an on/off toggle in Ollama/LM Studio provides.
build_effort: Speculative decoding on the existing llama-server backend: small-to-medium -- mostly passing `--spec-draft-model`/`--spec-type`/`-md` flags AgentDyno already controls, plus draft-pair selection logic and a benchmark harness. A full MLX backend: medium-to-large -- a new Apple-Silicon-only process manager, an mlx-lm dependency and MLX model-format handling (distinct from GGUF), routing through the 8403 gateway, and ongoing maintenance of a third engine. The verification/benchmark harness is the reusable, highest-leverage piece and is small-to-medium on its own.
risk_or_caveat: Speculative gains are inconsistent and can regress below baseline (fetched evidence: zero speedup for Gemma-2 pairs, useless drafts above ~1.5-3B, small ~1.4x on general text), so promising 'faster' can backfire unless AgentDyno measures per-machine. MLX is Apple-only, narrowing the feature to Mac users and adding a platform-specific code path. mlx-lm's own docs say its server is 'not recommended for production,' so leaning on it as a serving backend has stability/security caveats. Differentiation is shrinking: speculative decoding is already exposed by llama.cpp directly and is reportedly shipping in Ollama/LM Studio-class tools, so the defensible edge is the empirical *verification* of speedup on real hardware, not merely 'having' speculative decoding. Maintaining a third backend alongside llama-server + Ollama is a recurring cost against uncertain payoff. [uncertain] Current 2026 adoption breadth of MLX/spec-decoding in consumer local-LLM tooling was inferred from search snippets, not fully fetched primary sources.
